entity: households that clear snow with snow blowers, and consumer and local reporters
business_impact: A national study of US emergency department records estimated 91,451 visits for snow blower injuries from 2003 through 2018, most of them at home. The most common way people were hurt was putting a hand into the chute, in 44.5% of cases; every amputation in the study came from a hand in the chute. Visits peaked on January and February weekends.

evidence.source: Loder RT, Solanki D, "Events Due to Snowblower Use Seen in US Emergency Departments From 2003 Through 2018," Cureus 12(12):e11836 (2020)

entity: home gardeners, and home, garden and local reporters
business_impact: University extension guidance describes a light freeze, 29 to 32°F, as cold enough to kill young and frost-tender plants, and a moderate freeze, 25 to 28°F, as cold enough to damage most plants. It advises covers that reach the ground and are anchored to trap heat from the soil, removed as soon as temperatures return to 32°F; sheets, towels, blankets and cardboard can be used in a pinch, and plastic should be avoided unless a frame holds it off the plants.
story_seed: A spring freeze of 28°F or colder, with highs well below normal, is in the {metro} forecast — a Weather Company meteorologist on how cold the night gets and how long it stays below freezing, for a story on protecting garden plants from a late freeze

evidence.source: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension, "Cold protection options for growing fruit and vegetables throughout the winter," CAES Field Report, January 11, 2023

entity: drivers, including hybrid and electric vehicle owners, and consumer and auto reporters
business_impact: Federal fuel economy guidance says that in city driving a conventional gasoline car's gas mileage is roughly 15% lower at 20°F than at 77°F, and as much as 24% lower on short trips of 3 to 4 miles. Hybrids can drop about 30% to 34%, and an electric vehicle's range can drop by 41%, with about two-thirds of the extra energy used to heat the cabin.
story_seed: Highs at or below 20°F, well below normal, are in the {metro} forecast — a Weather Company meteorologist on how long the cold lasts, for a story on what cold weather does to gas mileage and electric vehicle range

evidence.source: U.S. Department of Energy and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, fueleconomy.gov, "Fuel Economy in Cold Weather"

entity: households preparing for power outages, and food, consumer and local reporters
business_impact: Federal preparedness guidance says to keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed in a power outage: a refrigerator keeps food cold for about four hours, and a full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours. It advises having nonperishable food and water, using coolers with ice if necessary and a thermometer to check temperatures, and throwing away food that has been at 40 degrees or higher for two hours or more.

evidence.source: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Ready.gov, "Power Outages" (last updated June 4, 2026)

entity: households that own or plan to buy portable generators, and consumer and local reporters
business_impact: Federal product safety officials say portable generators are one of the leading causes of carbon monoxide deaths after storms, and that the safest time to prepare is before the power goes out: test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, review generator instructions, and look for generators with a carbon monoxide shut-off feature. Generators should be used only outdoors, at least 20 feet from homes and buildings, with the exhaust pointed away from windows, doors and vents.
